extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in 19th-century maritime and emigration history
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive account of rules, customs, accommodation standards, provisioning, and daily routines aboard mid‑19th century emigrant ships (exemplified by the ship Eagle). Includes measurements, schedules, crew/passenger roles, and ventilation/catering arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passenger divisions and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Passengers are divided into four leading divisions: cabin passengers; saloon or house on deck passengers; second cabin passengers; 'tween deck and intermediate/third class passengers (sub‑divided into enclosed and open berths). Cabin and saloon passengers have exclusive right to the poop; ladies from the 'tween decks may be allowed to walk on it by the captain's kindness. 'Tween deck passengers may walk on the spar deck from the poop to the bow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies hierarchical passenger classes and their movement/space privileges aboard ship; indicates segregation of sexes in certain berths (young ladies grouped on one side, young men on the opposite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Berth dimensions and allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabin berths are 8 ft 2 by 5 ft 6 for two persons (with some double berths for families); second cabin on deck berths are 6 ft by 4 ft 6 for two persons; second cabin 'tween deck sleeping berths divided into closed (for families and single ladies) and open (exclusively occupied by single men); intermediate compartments for single people may contain 8 beds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete berth sizes and intended occupants by class/family status—used to assess accommodation adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mess organization and sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: After a few days at sea the purser arranges 'tween deck passengers into messes and issues a card naming the mess and a printed list of weekly provisions per adult. In second cabin 'tween decks each mess consists of 24 adults; enclosed intermediate 12; open 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines how food provisioning and social units are organized; indicates scale of communal provisioning for rationing and administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messmen election and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Each mess elects two messmen for one week. Messmen go to the purser to receive weekly provisions, fetch daily water, divide it to individuals if required, and must make puddings three times a week, as well as oatmeal cakes, loaf bread, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies passenger self‑management duties and expectations for communal meal preparation in lower classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of utensils and attendance by class
rubrics_metrics.description: Passengers in cabin and second cabin on deck provide nothing but bed, bedding and napery. Second cabin 'tween decks passengers provide bed, bedding, napery and a small cask or tin bottle to hold daily fresh water. In the intermediate no attendance is provided and passengers must supply bags/dishes and a dish to bring food from the cook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies differential service levels: higher classes are fully attended; lower classes must supply utensils and containers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water allowance and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fresh water is served out by the third mate to every messman once a day. Each adult is allowed three pints per day and the same allowance is given to the cook for the tea, coffee, soup, etc., for each person on board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines strict per‑person water rationing and the officer responsible for distribution—important for health and provisioning planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily hours: lights out and wakeup
rubrics_metrics.description: Lights must be put out by 10 p.m.; one light is allowed to burn all night in each division. Passengers not going to bed at 10 p.m. must go on deck or remain below in darkness and must not make noise that would disturb those in bed. Each passenger is expected to turn out of bed at 6 a.m.; the doctor generally comes round in the morning to see that all are up, especially in hot weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes curfew/quiet hours and a schedule for waking—rules intended to maintain order, rest, and medical oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meal times and dining rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Breakfast at 8 o'clock, dinner at 1, and tea at 6. As all messes cannot dine at once they take it week about in rotation (e.g., messes 1, 3 and 5 may be first one week and last the next).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets fixed meal schedule and a fair rotation system for access to galley service/dining space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galley arrangement and cooking duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The ship has two galleys, two cooks and four assistants. Provisions used in the first cabin, house on deck and second cabin 'tween decks are cooked in the starboard galley; those used by the third cabin or intermediate passengers and crew in the larboard galley. The first cabin has exclusive stewards and stewardess who attend passengers and are supplied with fresh provisions daily; second cabin has two stewards; second cabin 'tween decks each mess is provided with a steward; intermediate has no attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies division of kitchen labor and staff allocation by passenger class—important for evaluating service quality and segregation of provisioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisioning rotation and service protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions are served out to each mess by the purser in rotation: he commences with the messes in the second cabin and follows a set order for tea, coffee, sugar, flour, oatmeal, rice and other articles, then serves the intermediate following the same order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlines the purser's methodical distribution sequence to ensure equitable provisioning across messes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly dietary scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed weekly menus for Second Cabin and Intermediate Cabin listing breakfast, dinner and tea/supper for each day (examples: Sunday—coffee, biscuits and butter; dinner preserved potatoes, preserved meat, plum duff; Saturday breakfast porridge with butter, molasses or sugar; dinner salt beef and rice with molasses & biscuits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides explicit menu expectations and frequency of items—used to evaluate nutritional provisioning and variety per class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bread and baking frequency for messes
rubrics_metrics.description: Each mess may have oatmeal cakes and loaf bread fired three or four times a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies frequency of fresh baking available to messes—indicator of provisioning quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washing days and laundry conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two days are set apart each week for washing clothes. If those washing have not saved up fresh or collected rain water, they must wash them in salt water. Clothes are dried by tying them in the rigging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines laundry schedule and acceptable practices given limited fresh water—practical hygiene standard for voyages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning berths and daily upkeep
rubrics_metrics.description: Stewards, besides scraping the floor, collect the slops of the mess every day. The floor of the intermediate saloon is scraped daily by the messes in rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies responsibilities for cleanliness split between crew and passengers to maintain hygiene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation standards and design
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eagle is classed A1 for ventilation. Ventilation is on the same plan as Cunard steamers: cabin saloon has two ventilators on deck (glazed at top and opening in the sides); sleeping berths ventilated by windows in the sides and openings above each door; saloon ventilated by a large skylight; 'tween decks have iron ventilators glazed on top; three hatchways and a ventilator on upper deck glazed on top; sliding windows on each side of main deck and space left at top of each berth. Vessel is lighted by these windows and dead lights during day; at night by lanterns in each compartment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives technical ventilation measures considered necessary for healthy voyages—includes multiple specific structural features and classification as 'A1.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting policy and personal lanterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The vessel is lighted by windows and dead lights in the deck during the day; at night by lanterns in each compartment and by lanterns belonging to private individuals. Lights must be put out by 10 p.m., but one is allowed to burn all night in each division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets limits on night lighting for safety and order while allowing minimal personal/compartment lighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquor and onboard purchases policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ale and porter are sold to the 'tween deck passengers from 10 to 12 a.m. Passengers must obtain an order from the captain to obtain wine or spirits. Provisions or groceries can be purchased at any hour of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies restricted sale hours for common alcoholic drinks, requires captain's permission for stronger drinks, and allows continuous access to provisions/groceries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luggage recommendations and storage
rubrics_metrics.description: Two small boxes (approx. 30 in x 19 in x 16 in) are preferable to a large one. One marked 'not wanted on the voyage' is placed in the hold and may be brought to deck every three weeks; the other for use on the voyage is placed under the owner's sleeping berth. A carpet or canvas bag with inside pockets is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice on packing and stowage to facilitate access and space management aboard ship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing recommendations for voyage
rubrics_metrics.description: Each passenger must have two suits of clothing: one for cold, the other for warm weather. Any old whole clothing is acceptable. Coarse blue cloth or fustian trousers with a short coat or jacket and vest stand the voyage well; light trousers (canvas or shepherd tartan) with an alpaca coat are good for warm weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises adequate layering and durable clothing types suitable for varied conditions on a long sea voyage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles for daily use (kit list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended personal articles: a knife, fork, table and teaspoon, a pen knife, a hook pot, a baking can, a tin pot capable of holding 2 or 3 gallons of water, a lantern, brushes, combs, a mirror and tooth and hair brushes with washing basin and a slop pail for each mess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies minimum personal and communal equipment to ensure comfort and self-sufficiency for messes/passengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purser's role in provisioning and passenger arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The purser arranges passengers into messes, issues cards with names and printed lists of provisions per adult per week, serves provisions in rotation to messes and administers distribution days (e.g., Friday for provisions in the 'Eagle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines administrative responsibilities for provisioning and passenger organization—critical for orderly food distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steward and stewardess staffing per class
rubrics_metrics.description: The first cabin is provided with three stewards and a stewardess who attend the passengers exclusively; second cabin on deck has two stewards; in the second cabin 'tween decks each mess has a steward; in the intermediate no attendance is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets expectations for level of service and staff presence by passenger class, informing service quality assessments.
